All without us knowing.

In a medium millions engage in every day.


That medium is video games.

Yet despite video games as a medium proving itself to be great commercially and in popular culture, its preservation leaves much to be desired.

Commercial success does not guarantee permanence.

Storefront removal is permanent for many players.

When a platform changes policy, a publisher exits a storefront, or a region stops hosting a title, access can vanish without warning.

Physical media is not immortal.

Discs, cartridges, and packaging age, degrade, and become harder to find, making long-term access far less reliable than the digital impression suggests.

Rights can change faster than culture.

Licensing shifts, copyright disputes, and publisher decisions can take a game off the market even when it remains culturally valuable.

Compatibility is a real preservation problem.

Even legally owned games can become unplayable as hardware ages, software ecosystems change, and emulation support becomes the only remaining path.

Many games are already gone.

Club Penguin (2005–2017)

What happened?

  • Club Penguin was a massively popular online multiplayer game launched in 2005.
  • Disney discontinued the original game on March 30, 2017.
  • Its original servers were shut down, making the official online experience inaccessible.
  • Although fan-made recreations emerged, these were not the original official service.

P.T. (2014–2015)

What happened?

  • P.T. was a playable teaser released on the PlayStation 4 in August 2014.
  • It was intended to promote Silent Hills, a planned game involving Hideo Kojima and Guillermo del Toro.
  • Following the cancellation of Silent Hills, Konami removed P.T. from the PlayStation Store in April 2015.
  • By May 2015, even players who had previously claimed the demo could no longer download it through the PlayStation Store.

Nintendo Wii Shop Channel (2006–2019)

What happened?

  • The Wii Shop Channel launched in December 2006.
  • It provided access to downloadable WiiWare titles, Virtual Console games, and other software.
  • Nintendo discontinued new purchases on January 30, 2019.
  • The channel's remaining services, including redownloading purchased software, were subsequently discontinued.

What actually disappears

Digital ownership and availability are not necessarily permanent. A publisher can withdraw a game from distribution, potentially making it inaccessible to future generations.

When a digital storefront disappears, access to games that were distributed exclusively through it becomes increasingly difficult to maintain.

1 out of 132 games released before 1980 had been reissued.

A single storefront closure can make hundreds of games disappear.

The closure of Nintendo's 3DS and Wii U eShops on March 27, 2023 provides an excellent real-world example.

Preservation is not only about access.

Losing games is one thing, but we are losing more than that.

We are losing access to an entire part of our cultural history.

A medium that shapes popular culture and generates billions in revenue still struggles to preserve its own history.

Real-world action

Stop Killing Games

A growing movement that pushes for preservation, transparency, and consumer rights around game access.

It shows that public pressure can influence how platforms, publishers, and policymakers think about long-term access.


stopkillinggames.com/en

The path forward

Preservation is already happening.

Archivists, communities, and advocates are already protecting games that might otherwise disappear.

The question is whether we help sustain that work before it is too late.
